summary: SVDV (SphereX Viewer and Data Visualizer) is a public web platform for exploring real infrared images from NASA’s SPHEREx mission. The challenge asks for a tool that shows SPHEREx images and how they change over time. SVDV does this with an interactive 3D sky viewer and a blink comparator that flips between observation epochs of the same region. Any patch of sky opens from a link with right ascension, declination and field of view, and users can switch between all 102 infrared bands. A backend queries NASA/IPAC IRSA, so new data can be added as it is released. Spectral analysis matches intensity peaks to molecules such as H₂O, CO₂ and CH₄, and an AI assistant writes plain-language reports. SPHEREx will image over a billion objects, far more than anyone can check by hand. SVDV lets anyone take part, and it presents every change as an unvalidated candidate.
details: We developed SVDV, a public web platform that makes real SPHEREx infrared sky data accessible and easier to explore through four integrated modules: a 3D sky viewer, a live NASA data service, a spectral analysis engine, and AI-generated educational reports. Built with React, TypeScript, WebGL, and a Python/FastAPI backend, the platform addresses the challenge by allowing users to explore SPHEREx observations, switch between its 102 infrared bands, navigate observation timelines, and compare images of the same region over time using a multi-epoch blink comparator. Data is retrieved directly from NASA/IPAC IRSA, making it easier to incorporate new data releases. This is important because SPHEREx maps the entire sky every six months across 102 near-infrared bands and is expected to observe more than a billion objects, making the identification of changes and moving celestial objects a massive task. Comparing observations over time helps identify potential comets, asteroids, Pluto-like objects, and brown dwarfs. By lowering the technical barrier and requiring no formal astronomy training, SVDV makes scientific exploration more accessible while presenting potential discoveries as candidates that can be further verified.
